# Worksheet: a thousand people, one at a time

**~50 minutes**

Every other session this week has been a population model. The state was a few
numbers, and an equation said how those numbers change. This session is different
in kind: the state is a thousand people, each one an object you can look at and
ask questions of, and the population curves are something you compute
*afterwards*.

An agent-based model has three parts:

- the **agents**, the individuals that act;
- the **environment**, the space they live in, which decides who is next to whom;
- the **rules**, what happens to an agent in one step, and what happens to the
  world once per step.

This worksheet builds them in that order, runs the model, and looks at it. The
[chapter](../../chapters/06-agent-based-models.qmd) develops the same model
without a space; here every person has a place on a grid and a set of neighbours.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

Worked solutions are posted at the end of each day. Run `git pull` to collect
them.

::: {.callout-note}
## Greek letters you can copy

`\gamma` followed by `Tab` gives `γ` at a Julia prompt, but that completion
often does not fire inside a Quarto file like this one. Copy what you need
from here, or insert it from the command palette with the Unicode Latex
extension described in [Setting up](../../setup.qmd#optional-extras).

| Symbol | Reads as | At a Julia prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `Δ` | capital delta | `\Delta` then `Tab` |
| `β` | beta | `\beta` then `Tab` |
| `γ` | gamma | `\gamma` then `Tab` |
| `₀` | subscript zero | `\_0` then `Tab` |

`Δt` is two characters: `Δ` followed by `t`.

A subscript is its own character too: `R₀` is `R` followed by `₀`.

Plain ASCII names work exactly as well if you prefer them.
:::

## Setup

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-setup
using Agents
using CairoMakie
using Distributions
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using Random
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

no_steps!(model) = nothing   # for demonstration grids that are never stepped

const N = 1000
const β = 0.05
const c = 10.0
const γ = 0.25
const horizon = 120.0

println("R₀ under mass action = ", β * c / γ)
```

The parameters are the same as every other session: a thousand people, ten
contacts per unit time, transmission probability $\beta = 0.05$ per contact with
an infectious person, and recovery at rate $\gamma = 0.25$.

---

## Part A — the three components (~8 min)

### The environment

The space decides who is next to whom, and it is the first thing to build.
Agents.jl offers grids, graphs, continuous space, and street maps. This model
uses a grid.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a1
space = GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev)
```

Three choices are worth reading slowly.

`GridSpaceSingle` holds **at most one agent per cell**. A $40\times25$ grid is
1000 cells, so the grid *is* the population: the same thousand people as every
other session, now with an address each.

`periodic = true` wraps the edges, so the left column is next to the right one
and nobody lives on a boundary with fewer neighbours than everyone else.

`metric = :chebyshev` is how distance is counted, which Part B is about.

### The agents

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a2
@agent struct Person(GridAgent{2})
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `@agent` is not a class

If you are arriving from R or Python you may read `Person(GridAgent{2})` as a
class inheriting from a base class. Julia does not work that way. Data live in
`struct` types and behaviour lives in functions, which are chosen by the types
of their arguments. A struct has no methods of its own.

What the `@agent` macro does is copy in the fields that a two-dimensional grid
agent needs, `id` and `pos`, and add the fields you asked for. `Person` inherits
no behaviour from `GridAgent{2}`, because there is none to inherit. The rules
arrive separately, as ordinary functions, in Part C.
:::

Each `Person` carries two statuses rather than one. That is deliberate, and
Part C says why.

### Putting people in the space

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a3
function initialize_model(seed; I0 = 10, radius = 2, Δt = 0.1)
    space = GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person, space;
        agent_step!, model_step!,
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt, radius = radius),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for position in positions(model)
        add_agent!(position, model; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:I0]
        model[id].status = :I
        model[id].next_status = :I
    end
    return model
end
```

`properties` is where model-wide numbers live, reachable inside the rules as
`model.β` and so on. `rng = StableRNG(seed)` gives the model its own random
stream, which is what makes a run reproducible.

The rules `agent_step!` and `model_step!` are named here before they exist. Julia
resolves them when the model runs, so Part C can still define them.

---

## Part B — the neighbourhood (~12 min)

The neighbourhood is the property that makes this a spatial model, so it is worth
being exact about. Two things decide it: how far you look (the **radius**) and
how distance is counted (the **metric**).

- `:chebyshev` counts a diagonal step as one step, so a radius of 1 is the eight
  cells surrounding a person, the square ring.
- `:euclidean` measures straight-line distance, giving a disc.
- `:manhattan` adds the horizontal and vertical steps, giving a diamond.

Set the radius and the metric that pick out the eight cells touching a person,
the neighbourhood usually called the Moore neighbourhood.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b1
# TODO: which radius and which metric give the eight cells around a person?
neighbourhood_radius = 2
neighbourhood_metric = :euclidean

function demo_grid(metric)
    demo = StandardABM(
        Person, GridSpaceSingle((9, 9); periodic = false, metric = metric);
        model_step! = no_steps!,   # this grid is only for looking at
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = 0.1, radius = 1),
        rng = StableRNG(1),
    )
    for position in positions(demo)
        add_agent!(position, demo; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    return demo
end

demo = demo_grid(neighbourhood_metric)
centre = (5, 5)
neighbourhood = collect(nearby_positions(centre, demo, neighbourhood_radius))

check("the neighbourhood holds eight cells", length(neighbourhood) == 8)
check("every one of them touches the centre cell",
      !isempty(neighbourhood) &&
      all(maximum(abs.(p .- centre)) == 1 for p in neighbourhood))

(; neighbourhood_radius, neighbourhood_metric, size = length(neighbourhood))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B, the Moore neighbourhood

```julia
neighbourhood_radius = 1
neighbourhood_metric = :chebyshev
```

A diagonal neighbour is one Chebyshev step away, the same as a neighbour directly
above, so radius 1 under that metric is the full ring of eight.
:::

The picture below shows why the metric matters. It is drawn with `abmplot`, the
plotting function Agents.jl provides for looking at a model.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-neighbourhood
#| fig-cap: "One person (black) on a nine-by-nine grid with the cells within Chebyshev radius 1 (dark red) and the further cells added at radius 2 (orange). Radius 1 is the eight people touching the focal person; radius 2 adds sixteen more, twenty-four in all."
picture = demo_grid(:chebyshev)
focal = picture[id_in_position(centre, picture)]
ring1 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, picture, 1))
ring2 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, picture, 2))

ring_colour(p) = p.id == focal.id ? :black :
                 p.id in ring1 ? :firebrick :
                 p.id in ring2 ? :orange : :lightgrey

fig, ax, _ = abmplot(picture; agent_color = ring_colour, agent_marker = :rect,
                     agent_size = 26, figure = (; size = (520, 520)))
hidedecorations!(ax)
ax.title = "Radius 1 and radius 2 under the Chebyshev metric"
fig
```

The model in Part C uses **radius 2**, so a contact is drawn from the
twenty-four people within two cells. Part D asks what that choice costs.

### Experiment: the edge of the world

`periodic = true` in `initialize_model` wraps the grid. Run the cell below to see
what a person in the corner would otherwise have.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b2
function corner_neighbours(periodic)
    grid = StandardABM(
        Person, GridSpaceSingle((9, 9); periodic = periodic, metric = :chebyshev);
        model_step! = no_steps!,
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = 0.1, radius = 1),
        rng = StableRNG(1),
    )
    for position in positions(grid)
        add_agent!(position, grid; status = :S, next_status = :S)
    end
    return length(collect(nearby_positions((1, 1), grid, 1)))
end

(; wrapped = corner_neighbours(true), with_edges = corner_neighbours(false))
```

### B1. Interpret

- With `periodic = false`, a person in the corner has fewer neighbours than a
  person in the middle. Nothing in the epidemic rules mentions corners, so where
  would that difference show up in the results, and why is wrapping the grid the
  simpler choice for this model?

## Part C — the rules (~18 min)

An agent-based model is defined by what one individual does in one step. Two
things happen to a person: a susceptible makes some contacts and may be infected
by one of them, and an infectious person may recover.

Both need a *rate* turned into a *probability over a step of length $\Delta t$*.
The contact side is given to you: a susceptible draws
$K\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\,\Delta t)$ contacts from its neighbourhood, each
of which transmits with probability $\beta$ if the person contacted happens to be
infectious.

For recovery, the waiting time is exponential with rate $\gamma$, exactly as in
the jump-process session, so the probability of having recovered by the end of one
step is $1-e^{-\gamma\Delta t}$.

Your two `# TODO`s are the recovery probability and the commit step.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c1
function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        neighbours = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, model.radius))
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbours)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I
        # TODO: recover with probability 1 - exp(-γ Δt) over this step
        if rand(abmrng(model)) < 0.0
            person.next_status = :R
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

function model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        # TODO: commit the status each person decided on during this step
    end
    return nothing
end

susceptible_count(model) = count(p.status == :S for p in allagents(model))
infected_count(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))
recovered_count(model) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(model))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C, the two rules

```julia
if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
```

and, inside the `model_step!` loop:

```julia
person.status = person.next_status
```

`abmrng(model)` is the model's own random stream. Using it rather than a global
`rand()` is what makes a seeded run reproducible. If the epidemic never gets
going, check the commit line: without it, nobody's status ever changes.
:::

`agent_step!` runs once for each person, `model_step!` once for the whole model
at the end of the step. Writing to `next_status` and copying it across afterwards
is what makes the update synchronous, and question C1 asks why that matters.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c2
function simulate(seed; I0 = 10, radius = 2, Δt = 0.1)
    steps = round(Int, horizon / Δt)
    _, data = run!(
        initialize_model(seed; I0, radius, Δt), steps;
        mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count],
        showprogress = false,
    )
    return Matrix(data[:, [
        :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count,
    ]])'
end

single_run = simulate(20250711)
step_times = collect(0.0:0.1:horizon)

check("every person has exactly one status at every step",
      maximum(abs.(vec(sum(single_run; dims = 1)) .- N)) == 0)
check("counts are whole people and never negative", minimum(single_run) >= 0)
check("the epidemic took off", single_run[3, end] > 100)
check("the epidemic has finished by the end of the run", single_run[2, end] == 0)

(; final_counts = single_run[:, end],
   peak = maximum(single_run[2, :]),
   peak_time = step_times[argmax(single_run[2, :])])
```

Now look at the population rather than the curves.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-snapshots
#| fig-cap: "The same run at three times. Susceptible people are blue, infectious red, recovered green. Infection stays in patches and leaves recovered people behind it, which is what a fixed neighbourhood does to an epidemic."
status_colour(p) = p.status === :S ? :steelblue :
                   p.status === :I ? :firebrick : :seagreen

snapshot_model = initialize_model(20250711)
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 250))
previous = 0.0
for (j, t) in enumerate((5.0, 20.0, 50.0))
    step!(snapshot_model, round(Int, (t - previous) / 0.1))
    previous = t
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t", aspect = DataAspect())
    abmplot!(ax, snapshot_model; agent_color = status_colour,
             agent_marker = :rect, agent_size = 7)
    hidedecorations!(ax)
end
fig
```

The deterministic SIR model is the reference to compare against. It assumes a
contact can be anybody in the population.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c3
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    b, contact, g, n = p
    infection = b * contact * u[1] * u[2] / n
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - g * u[2]
    du[3] = g * u[2]
    return nothing
end

ode_solution = solve(
    ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, horizon), (β, c, γ, N)),
    Tsit5(); saveat = step_times,
)
ode_states = Array(ode_solution)

(; abm_peak = maximum(single_run[2, :]),
   ode_peak = round(maximum(ode_states[2, :]); digits = 1),
   abm_final = single_run[3, end],
   ode_final = round(ode_states[3, end]; digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-curves
#| fig-cap: "Three seeded runs of the grid model (solid) against the deterministic SIR trajectory (dashed). The three runs differ from each other, and all three fall well short of the ODE."
seeds = 20250711 .+ (0:2)
replicates = [simulate(seed) for seed in seeds]

fig = Figure(size = (900, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious people",
          title = "Three runs on the grid, and the well-mixed ODE")
for (k, run) in enumerate(replicates)
    lines!(ax, step_times, run[2, :]; color = (:firebrick, 0.8), linewidth = 2,
           label = k == 1 ? "grid model" : nothing)
end
lines!(ax, step_times, ode_states[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash,
       linewidth = 2, label = "ODE")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### Experiment: the timestep is part of the model

`Δt` here is not a solver tolerance. In the ODE sessions the timestep was a
numerical detail the solver chose and refined until it stopped mattering. In this
model it sets how many contacts a person makes per step and how often anyone can
recover, so it belongs to the model definition. Change it and re-run.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c4
coarse_run = simulate(20250711; Δt = 1.0)

(; Δt_01 = (; peak = maximum(single_run[2, :]), final = single_run[3, end]),
   Δt_1 = (; peak = maximum(coarse_run[2, :]), final = coarse_run[3, end]))
```

### C1. Interpret

- `agent_step!` writes to `next_status` and `model_step!` copies it across
  afterwards. Suppose it wrote to `person.status` directly instead. What could
  then happen within a single step that should not, and what would the answer
  start to depend on?
- The three runs in the figure differ from each other, and all of them fall well
  short of the ODE. Those are two different kinds of disagreement. Which one
  would more replicates fix, and which one would survive any number of them?
- At $\Delta t = 1$ a person makes ten contacts before anybody can recover.
  Using the numbers from the last cell, say whether the coarse step is a
  numerical error, a changed assumption about how people meet, or both.

> *Your answer here.*

## Part D — how much the neighbourhood matters (~12 min)

Everything so far started with ten infectious people spread over the grid. Real
outbreaks start with one, and then whether anything happens at all is a matter of
chance.

Two hundred introductions of a single case, each with its own seed, at two
contact radii: radius 1, the eight people touching you, and radius 2, the
twenty-four within two cells. Your `# TODO` is to classify the outcomes.

A *final* size means the epidemic has finished, so each model runs until nobody
is infectious rather than stopping at a fixed time.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-d1
#| error: true
introduction_seeds = 9000 .+ (1:200)

function final_size(seed; radius = 2, I0 = 1, Δt = 0.1, max_steps = 6000)
    model = initialize_model(seed; I0, radius, Δt)
    for _ in 1:max_steps
        infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model)
        step!(model, 1)
    end
    error("epidemic still infectious after $max_steps steps; increase max_steps " *
          "(if Part C's model_step! is still unfinished, complete that first)")
end

final_sizes = Dict(radius => [final_size(seed; radius) for seed in introduction_seeds]
                   for radius in (1, 2))

# TODO: true for the runs that fizzled out — use a cutoff of 100 total infections
fizzled = Dict(radius => falses(length(final_sizes[radius])) for radius in (1, 2))

fizzle_fraction = Dict(radius => mean(fizzled[radius]) for radius in (1, 2))
mass_action_prediction = γ / (β * c)

check("at radius 2 the fizzle fraction is near the mass-action 1/R₀",
      abs(fizzle_fraction[2] - mass_action_prediction) < 0.1)
check("at radius 1 it is nowhere near it",
      fizzle_fraction[1] - mass_action_prediction > 0.3)

(; mass_action_prediction,
   fizzle_radius_1 = fizzle_fraction[1],
   fizzle_radius_2 = fizzle_fraction[2])
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part D, classifying outcomes

```julia
fizzled = Dict(radius => final_sizes[radius] .< 100 for radius in (1, 2))
```

The dot makes the comparison element by element, giving a vector of
`true`/`false`. `.!fizzled[radius]` then negates it, which is how the next cell
picks out the runs that took off.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-d2
#| error: true
took_off = Dict(radius => .!fizzled[radius] for radius in (1, 2))

summary_by_radius = [(; radius,
    neighbours = (2radius + 1)^2 - 1,
    fizzle_fraction = round(fizzle_fraction[radius]; digits = 3),
    mean_if_it_takes_off = any(took_off[radius]) ?
        round(mean(final_sizes[radius][took_off[radius]]); digits = 1) : nothing,
    mean_over_all_runs = round(mean(final_sizes[radius]); digits = 1))
    for radius in (1, 2)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-introductions
#| error: true
#| fig-cap: "Final epidemic size across 200 introductions of a single infectious person, at contact radius 1 and radius 2. Widening the neighbourhood by one cell changes the outcome from an outbreak that almost never establishes to one that establishes about half the time."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
for (j, radius) in enumerate((1, 2))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; xlabel = "final number recovered", ylabel = "runs",
              title = "contact radius $radius")
    hist!(ax, Float64.(final_sizes[radius]); bins = 40, color = (:steelblue, 0.8))
end
fig
```

### D1. Interpret

- At radius 2 the fizzle fraction lands close to $1/R_0 = 0.5$, the value the
  branching-process argument from the jump-process session predicts. At radius 1
  it does not. The parameters $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ are identical in both, so
  $\beta c/\gamma$ is 2 in both. What has changed, and what does that tell you
  about calling $\beta c/\gamma$ this model's $R_0$?
- Compare `mean_if_it_takes_off` with `mean_over_all_runs` at radius 2. One of
  those two numbers describes no run that happened. Which, and why?
- Parts A to C started from ten cases spread over the grid and showed none of
  this. Why did the effect disappear there, and what does that tell you about
  when an individual-level model is worth its cost?

> *Your answer here.*
